question.:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=4 y$ along the curve parametrized by $r(t)=\langle t^{2},t\rangle$ for $t\in [0,\sqrt{6}].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(t^{2})\,i+(t)\,j$, then along the curve we have $x=t^{2}$, $y=t$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =(2 t)\,i+(1)\,j \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(2 t)^2+(1)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=4 y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4)(t) \\  & =4 t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{6}}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{6}}(4 t)(\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=4 t^{2} + 1$, $\text{d}u=(8 t)\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{6}}4 t \sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{25}\frac{1}{2}\cdot u^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\big|_{1}^{25} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(25)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(125)-(1)] \\  & =\left(\frac{125}{3}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \\  & =\frac{124}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle \int_C 3 x y - 3 z^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\langle t^{2}, 2 t + 1, 3 t + 1\rangle$ for $\frac{1}{2}\le t\le \frac{3}{2}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $r(t)=\langle t^{2}, 2 t + 1, 3 t + 1\rangle,$ then along the curve we have $x=t^{2}$, $y=2 t + 1$, $z=3 t + 1$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j+\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\,k \\ &= \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t^{2})i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 t + 1)j+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 t + 1)k \\ &= (2 t)\,i+(2)\,j+(3)\,k \\ \|r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\ &= \sqrt{(2 t)^2+(2)^2+(3)^2} \\ &= \sqrt{4 t^{2} + 13}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=3 x y - 3 z^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t))&=3\left((t^{2})(2 t + 1)-(3 t + 1)^2\right) \\ &= 3\left(2t^3+(1)t^2-\left(9t^2+(6)t+1\right)\right) \\ &= 6 t^{3} - 24 t^{2} - 18 t - 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f(x,y,z)\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\frac{3}{2}} f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &= \int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\frac{3}{2}}(6 t^{3} - 24 t^{2} - 18 t - 3)(\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 13})\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &= \int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\frac{3}{2}}\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 13} \left(6 t^{3} - 24 t^{2} - 18 t - 3\right)\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

At $(1,1,1)$, the exponential is $e^{1(1)-1}=1$ and $x+y=x+z=2$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla h(1,1,1)&=\left\langle 1+2(1)+\frac12,\,1-2,\,2(1)+\frac12\right\rangle\\
&=\left\langle \frac72,-1,\frac52\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Negate all three components:

$$
-\nabla h(1,1,1)=\left\langle -\frac72,1,-\frac52\right\rangle.
$$

Thus $h$ decreases most rapidly in this direction. Multiplying this vector by a positive number does not change its direction.

question.:question/problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)=2x^2-3y^2$. What is the rate of change of $g$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf v=\langle 4,-3\rangle$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change is the directional derivative $D_{\mathbf u}g(1,1)$, where $\mathbf u$ is the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v$.

First normalize the direction vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathbf v\|&=\sqrt{4^2+(-3)^2}=5,\\
\mathbf u&=\left\langle\frac45,-\frac35\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Next compute the gradient and evaluate it at the given point:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla g(x,y)&=\langle 4x,-6y\rangle,\\
\nabla g(1,1)&=\langle 4,-6\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally take the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathbf u}g(1,1)&=\nabla g(1,1)\cdot\mathbf u\\
&=4\left(\frac45\right)+(-6)\left(-\frac35\right)\\
&=\frac{16+18}{5}=\frac{34}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The positive sign means that $g$ increases in this direction.

question.:question/problem:
At a point $P$, a differentiable function $f(x,y)$ has gradient $\nabla f(P)=\langle 2,-1\rangle$.

Which expression gives the rate of change of $f$ at $P$ in the direction of $\mathbf v=\langle 3,4\rangle$? You do not need to evaluate the expression.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change in a direction is the directional derivative

$$
D_{\mathbf u}f(P)=\nabla f(P)\cdot\mathbf u,
$$

where $\mathbf u$ is a unit vector in the specified direction. Since $\|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$,

$$
\mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|}=\left\langle\frac35,\frac45\right\rangle.
$$

Thus the required expression is

$$
\langle 2,-1\rangle\cdot\left\langle\frac35,\frac45\right\rangle
=\frac{2(3)+(-1)(4)}{5}.
$$

Dividing by $5$ makes the rate a change per unit distance; using $\mathbf v$ without normalizing would give a rate for a different speed of travel.

question.:question/problem: Consider the function $f(x,y)=2xy+e^{2x-y}$. What is the signed rate of change of $f$ at the point $(1,2)$ in the direction in which the function decreases most rapidly?
question.:question/worked-solution:
First compute the gradient, using the chain rule for the exponential term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=2y+2e^{2x-y},\\
f_y(x,y)&=2x-e^{2x-y},\\
\nabla f(1,2)&=\langle 4+2,2-1\rangle=\langle 6,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

The direction of steepest decrease is opposite to the gradient. The corresponding unit vector is

$$
\mathbf u=-\frac{\nabla f(1,2)}{\|\nabla f(1,2)\|}
=\frac{\langle-6,-1\rangle}{\sqrt{37}}.
$$

The rate in that direction is

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathbf u}f(1,2)&=\langle6,1\rangle\cdot\frac{\langle-6,-1\rangle}{\sqrt{37}}\\
&=\frac{-36-1}{\sqrt{37}}=-\sqrt{37}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, $D_{\mathbf u}f=\|\nabla f\|\cos\theta$ is smallest when $\theta=\pi$. The magnitude of the decrease is $\sqrt{37}$, but the signed rate of change is $-\sqrt{37}$.

question.:question/problem:
A body of mass $2\,\text{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons.
At time $t\ge 0$ seconds, the velocity of the body is given by $v(t)=2{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-36t+2$ meters per second.
Calculate the time at which the force acting on the body has zero magnitude.
question.:question/worked-solution:
According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration. 

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-36t+2) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-6t-36\end{aligned}
$$

Since the mass is always positive, the force has zero magnitude when the acceleration equals zero. So, we set $a(t)=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{t}^{2}-6t-36 & =0 \\ {t}^{2}-t-6 & =0 \\ (t-3)(t+2) & =0 \\ t & =-2,\,3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\ge 0,$ we disregard the negative solution. 

Therefore, the force has zero magnitude at $t=3\,\text{s}.$

question.:question/problem:
A body of mass $1.5\,\text{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons.
At time $t\ge 0$ seconds, the position of the body is given by $s(t)=2{t}^{3}-12{t}^{2}+t-5$ meters per second.
Calculate the time at which the force acting on the body has zero magnitude.
question.:question/worked-solution:
According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration. 

To find the velocity $v(t),$ we differentiate the displacement $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-12{t}^{2}+t-5) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-24t+1\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}-24t+1) \\  & =12t-24\end{aligned}
$$

Since the mass is always positive, the force has zero magnitude when the acceleration equals zero. So, we set $a(t)=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}12t-24 & =0 \\ 12 & =24 \\ t & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force has zero magnitude at $t=2\,\text{s}.$
